Dual momentum - sectors with an absolute filter and volatility targeting

Statistical validation   5032 observations · 252 periods per year

Is the measured edge distinguishable from luck, and does it survive honest accounting? This report says nothing about how the backtest was built; the engine analysis is what asks that.

Materially weakened

This tool falsifies; it cannot validate. It finds reasons to disbelieve a backtest, never reasons to believe one. The findings below are what the tests actually established. Nothing here says the strategy cannot work - only that this backtest does not show that it does.

Findings (2)

High Returns are explained by factor exposure ATTR-LEVERED-BETA

The returns are explained by exposures you can buy directly: alpha is 0.47% a year with a t-statistic of 0.30 (p=0.764) and the factors explain 66% of the variance.

What to do: Hedge the factor exposures and re-test the residual, which is the only part that could be alpha.
High The selection procedure does not generalise SELECT-HIGH-PBO

PBO is 59.1% across 12870 splits: the in-sample winner lands in the bottom half out-of-sample more often than not, and loses money in 0.1% of them.

What to do: Simplify the strategy until the parameter space is small enough to defend, or select on economic reasoning rather than on backtest performance.

What could not be tested

  • Matched-exposure random-entry test: the position series is multi-asset. This test asks whether a single instrument was timed well, and reordering a cross-sectional book in time does not answer that question.

Headline

Every Sharpe ratio on this page is annualised to 252 periods unless the row says otherwise. Every one of them is also computed on returns in excess of the risk-free rate (1.56% a year over this sample), and the benchmark is treated identically. Total return, drawdown and Calmar are left on total returns, because those describe the path an investor lived through.

The book is on average 65% invested. If the backtest did not credit the idle balance at the bill rate, the return series understates by about 0.54% a year - in the opposite direction to the adjustment above, and worth checking before reading the excess figures as final.

MeasureValue95% interval
Annualised Sharpe (naive annualisation) 0.54 0.16 to 0.95
Autocorrelation-adjusted (Lo 2002) 0.65 0.19 to 1.14
Per-period Sharpe0.0340 0.0100 to 0.0595

The interval is a stationary bootstrap with a Politis-White block length of 20.7 over 2000 resamples - not the analytic standard error, which assumes away the serial dependence these returns have.

Lo's adjustment moves the annualisation factor from 15.87 to 19.12, raising the annualised Sharpe by 20.4%: these returns are negatively autocorrelated at short lags, so naive sqrt(q) annualisation was too harsh.

Caveat: annualising to 252 periods implies a sum over 251 lags, but 5032 observations can only speak to about 76; the adjustment assumes no dependence beyond that, and cannot rule out longer-horizon persistence.

Attribution: is the edge just factor exposure?

Regression of excess strategy returns on the Fama-French factors. Alpha is the intercept - what is left once the factors are accounted for. A p-value above 0.05 means the strategy has not been shown to add anything the factors do not already explain.

R-squared 66.4% over 5032 observations. Standard errors: Newey-West HAC, 76 lags. Regression residuals from a return series are serially correlated, and plain OLS standard errors would understate the uncertainty on alpha - the one coefficient the whole exercise turns on.

How much of this was the path it took?

Maximum drawdown is an extreme-value statistic, and one realisation of it says much less than it appears to. These are the same returns resampled in blocks, so the distributions show how different the headline figures could plausibly have been on another draw of the same process.

StatisticRealised Resampled median5th to 95th percentile Realised percentile
Total return 319.33% 307.19% 96.83% to 727.02% 53%
Annualised Sharpe 0.54 0.53 0.21 to 0.86 52%
Maximum drawdown -27.13% -27.13% -40.11% to -16.45% 45%
Drawdown a matched random walk would expect -25.54% same drift and volatility IID normal, no fat tails 42%

Both comparisons understate, and in opposite ways. block resampling with a mean block of 20.7 periods cannot reassemble drawdowns that unfolded over much longer horizons, so the resampled distribution understates how deep a drawdown this strategy can produce. The matched random walk assumes IID normal returns, so it has neither volatility clustering nor fat tails and will also come out shallower than reality. A realised drawdown far outside both means the loss came from the order in which returns arrived, and neither baseline can recreate it.

Selection bias

t-statistic BHY needs at 54 trials 3.06 · annualised Sharpe 0.83
Rank of this result among the trials 11 of 54 by t-statistic

Deflation runs on returns net of 3 bps, the upper end of realistic cost for US large-cap ETFs, so this figure sits slightly below the gross Sharpe in the headline. Trial-Sharpe dispersion measured from 54 trial columns. Sharpe ratios in this table are per-period because that is the scale the Deflated Sharpe is defined on; scaling both sides would not change the comparison.

The two selection tests here answer different questions and can disagree. The Deflated Sharpe asks whether this result beats the best of 54 draws from a no-edge null; the Harvey-Liu BHY haircut asks whether the t-statistic survives a false-discovery correction across 54 tests. They disagree on this sample: the Deflated Sharpe clears its bar at 0.965 while BHY takes the t-statistic to 1.16 (p = 0.245), which is not significant. Read the selection-bias conclusion as unsettled rather than passed: one of the two standard corrections does not clear it.

The trial count prices the configurations declared for this backtest. An effect taken from published work arrives with a search history of its own - the papers that found it, and the ones that were never written - and nothing in this report can see that. Read 54 as a floor on the number of things that were tried, not as the number of things that were tried.

Simulated null: the observed result sits at the 99.5% percentile of 1500 replications (p = 0.005). Validity check: the simulation and the closed form disagree by 24.9% - trial Sharpes have fatter tails than the normal approximation assumes, so the analytic Deflated Sharpe under-penalises and the real bar is higher.

The degradation slope is deliberately not reported as evidence, and neither is the in-sample-against-out-of-sample scatter that usually accompanies this chart. CSCV splits one fixed sample into complementary halves, so the two Sharpes sum to a constant: the scatter falls on a line of slope near -1 whatever the strategy does, and the apparent decay is an identity rather than a finding. The right-hand panel shows what the winner actually earns out of sample instead.

Robustness

TestResultReading
Annualised Sharpe, low / high volatility 0.57 / 0.54 same sign
Annualised Sharpe across 20 start dates 0.54 to 0.73 stable
Profit concentration vs a normal baseline 1.31x as expected
Annualised Sharpe dropping the best 1% / 5% of periods -0.02 / -1.43 from 0.54
Sign-flip randomisation p-value 0.003 signal informative
Parameter neighbourhood retention 90.3% plateau

The post-drop Sharpe falls steeply for almost any strategy - removing the best 5% of periods from a Sharpe-0.54 series is expected to push it below zero, which is why the concentration ratio, not the post-drop Sharpe, is what this test actually reads. A ratio near 1.0 means the profit is no more concentrated than the Sharpe alone implies.

Universe: not established. Survivorship leaves no trace in a return series, so this question stays open.
